pharm: Competitively inhibits cholinesterase, reducing acetylcholine breakdown so that acetylcholine accumulates at the neuromuscular junction and competes with nondepolarizing blocking agents to restore neuromuscular transmission
quick: 0.03-0.07 mg/kg IV (max 0.07 mg/kg or 5 mg, whichever is less), with atropine/glycopyrrolate
Use only if clearly needed; may cause uterine irritability near term
Unknown if excreted in milk; weigh benefit versus risk
Half-life prolonged in renal impairment; titrate and monitor
Not studied; levels may rise with impaired hepatic function
Train-of-four (peripheral nerve stimulator), heart rate, BP, ventilation
summary: Neostigmine methylsulfate injection is a reversible cholinesterase inhibitor indicated for reversal of the effects of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents after surgery. It must be given by trained providers with a peripheral nerve stimulator (train-of-four) to guide dosing, and an anticholinergic agent (atropine or glycopyrrolate) should be given before or with it to limit bradycardia. The usual dose range is 0.03 to 0.07 mg/kg IV.
indications: Reversal of the effects of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBA) after surgery

dosage.c: Adult - shorter-acting NMBA / first twitch well above 10% of baseline or second twitch present
dosage.t: Single dose; redose guided by train-of-four
dosage.n: Give with anticholinergic (atropine ~15 mcg/kg or glycopyrrolate ~10 mcg/kg)

dosage.c: Adult - longer-acting NMBA / first twitch close to 10% of baseline
dosage.t: Single dose; redose guided by train-of-four
dosage.n: Maximum total dose 0.07 mg/kg or up to 5 mg, whichever is less

dosage.d: Atropine sulfate ~15 mcg/kg IV or glycopyrrolate ~10 mcg/kg IV
dosage.t: Several minutes before or concomitantly (separate syringes)
dosage.n: Lessens risk of bradycardia from neostigmine

admin: Administer by intravenous route only, by trained healthcare providers familiar with NMBAs
Ensure adequate ventilation and a patent airway until full recovery of spontaneous respiration
Use a peripheral nerve stimulator (train-of-four) to time dosing and assess recovery
Require at least a 10% twitch response to the first TOF stimulus before administering
Give an anticholinergic (atropine or glycopyrrolate) before or with neostigmine
Reduce the dose if recovery from neuromuscular blockade is nearly complete
moa: Neostigmine methylsulfate is a competitive cholinesterase inhibitor. By reducing the breakdown of acetylcholine, it increases acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft; the accumulated acetylcholine competes for the same binding site as nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents and reverses the neuromuscular blockade.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to neostigmine methylsulfate (reactions have included urticaria, angioedema, erythema multiforme, rash, facial/peripheral swelling, pyrexia, flushing, hypotension, bronchospasm, bradycardia, anaphylaxis)
Peritonitis or mechanical obstruction of the urinary or intestinal tracts
relative: Known cardiac disease, cardiac arrhythmias, or recent coronary artery occlusion (heightened sensitivity to hemodynamic effects)
Myasthenia gravis (increased risk of cardiovascular complications)
monitor: Continuous blood pressure and ECG in patients with cardiac disease
Train-of-four response to avoid neuromuscular dysfunction from overdose

preg: There are no adequate or well-controlled studies in pregnant women; it is not known whether neostigmine can cause fetal harm. Anticholinesterase drugs, including neostigmine, may cause uterine irritability and induce premature labor when administered near term. Neostigmine methylsulfate injection should be given to a pregnant woman only if clearly needed.
lact: It is not known whether neostigmine methylsulfate is excreted in human milk. Because many drugs are excreted in human milk and because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, a decision should be made whether to discontinue nursing or the drug, considering the importance of the drug to the mother.
renal: Elimination half-life is prolonged in renal impairment (about 79.8 min in normal subjects, 104.7 min in transplant patients, and 181 min in anephric patients). Titrate carefully and monitor recovery in patients with impaired renal function.
hepatic: The pharmacokinetics of neostigmine in hepatic impairment have not been studied. Neostigmine is metabolized by microsomal liver enzymes, and its concentration may increase in patients with impaired hepatic function.

major: Depolarizing muscle relaxants (e.g. succinylcholine) - neostigmine reversal not recommended; may prolong phase-1 block
moderate: Certain antibiotics (neomycin, streptomycin, kanamycin) have nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking action - neostigmine dose adjustment may be required
Drugs that inhibit or induce hepatic metabolizing enzymes or transporters may alter neostigmine concentration - monitor longer
interactions.diagnostics: Muscle twitch (train-of-four) response should be monitored; cholinergic effects may confound assessment

serious: Cardiac arrhythmias and nonspecific ECG changes
rare: Hypersensitivity reactions including angioedema and erythema multiforme
emergency: Cholinergic crisis (increasing muscle weakness involving respiratory muscles, may be fatal)

monitoring: Train-of-four response via peripheral nerve stimulator before and after dosing
Adequacy of spontaneous ventilation and airway patency
Continuous BP and ECG in patients with cardiovascular disease
counsel: This medicine is given by injection during or after anaesthesia in a monitored setting
It reverses the effect of muscle relaxants used during surgery
Another medicine (atropine or glycopyrrolate) is given with it to protect your heart rate
Your breathing, heart rate, and muscle strength will be watched closely until you recover
pk: Antagonism of neuromuscular block within minutes of IV dosing
Approximately 24 to 113 minutes after IV injection (prolonged in renal impairment)
Effect titrated to recovery of neuromuscular function; redose guided by train-of-four
Store as directed on the product labeling; protect per manufacturer instructions
pearls: Always co-administer an anticholinergic (atropine or glycopyrrolate) to blunt neostigmine-induced bradycardia and muscarinic effects
Require at least 10% twitch recovery (train-of-four) before giving neostigmine; it is ineffective against deep block
Giving large doses when block is already minimal can cause paradoxical neuromuscular dysfunction
Not for reversing depolarizing agents like succinylcholine - it may prolong phase-1 block
Overdose causes cholinergic crisis (muscle and respiratory weakness); treat by stopping anticholinesterases and giving atropine, support ventilation
missed: Not applicable - neostigmine methylsulfate injection is administered by a clinician during or after anaesthesia, not on a fixed self-administered schedule.
overdose: Overdose produces muscarinic symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, increased bronchial and salivary secretions, bradycardia), managed with additional atropine or glycopyrrolate. It may cause a cholinergic crisis characterized by increasing muscle weakness that, through involvement of respiratory muscles, can be fatal if not promptly treated. Treatment includes immediate withdrawal of all anticholinesterase medication, immediate use of atropine, and support of ventilation. Cholinergic crisis must be distinguished from myasthenic crisis (e.g. with edrophonium and clinical judgment) because their treatments differ radically.
